title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
text: Sentence-BERT uses siamese and triplet network structures to produce sentence embeddings. Semantic similarity search compares these embeddings using cosine similarity. Encoding sentences separately avoids repeatedly processing every possible sentence pair through BERT, making similarity search more efficient.

title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
text: Dense Passage Retrieval addresses passage selection for open-domain question answering. A dual-encoder framework learns dense representations for questions and passages. The retriever selects relevant passages from a corpus for a downstream question-answering system. The paper compares dense retrieval with traditional lexical retrieval such as BM25.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines a pretrained sequence-to-sequence model with an external dense vector index of Wikipedia. A neural retriever provides documents that supply evidence for generation. The paper studies variants that condition on retrieved passages across an output sequence or separately at each generated token. External retrieval supplements knowledge stored in model parameters.

title: REALM: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model Pre-Training
text: REALM incorporates a latent knowledge retriever into language-model pre-training. The retriever accesses documents from a large corpus such as Wikipedia during pre-training, fine-tuning, and inference. Masked language modeling supplies a learning signal for training the retriever without supervised retrieval labels. The work evaluates the approach on open-domain question answering.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
text: Lost in the Middle investigates how language models use information inside long contexts. Experiments include multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval. Model performance can depend on where relevant information appears: information near the beginning or end is often used more successfully than information in the middle. A large context window alone does not guarantee robust use of all context.
